title: Latin square
text:
The Korean mathematician Choi Seok-jeong was the first to publish an example of Latin squares of order nine, in order to construct a magic square in 1700, predating Leonhard Euler by 67 years.[1]

### Counting

This account follows .[2]

The counting of Latin squares has a long history, but the published accounts contain many errors. Euler in 1782,[3] and Cayley in 1890,[4] both knew the number of reduced Latin squares up to order five. In 1915, MacMahon[5] approached the problem in a different way, but initially obtained the wrong value for order five. M.Frolov in 1890,[6] and Tarry in 1901,[7,8] found the number of reduced squares of order six. M. Frolov gave an incorrect count of reduced squares of order seven. R.A. Fisher and F. Yates,[9] unaware of earlier work of E. Schönhardt,[10] gave the number of isotopy classes of orders up to six. In 1939, H. W. Norton found 562 isotopy classes of order seven,[11] but acknowledged that his method was incomplete. A. Sade, in 1951,[12] but privately published earlier in 1948, and P. N. Saxena[13] found more classes and, in 1966, D. A. Preece noted that this corrected Norton's result to 564 isotopy classes.[14] However, in 1968, J. W. Brown announced an incorrect value of 563,[15] which has often been repeated. He also gave the wrong number of isotopy classes of order eight. The correct number of reduced squares of order eight had already been found by M. B. Wells in 1967,[16] and the numbers of isotopy classes, in 1990, by G. Kolesova, C.W.H. Lam and L. Thiel.[17] The number of reduced squares for order nine was obtained by S. E. Bammel and J. Rothstein,[18] for order 10 by B. D. McKay and E. Rogoyski,[19] and for order 11 by B. D. McKay and I. M. Wanless.[20]
